name: 1914 Plant City High School Community Center
summary: Plant City's original 1914 high school building on North Collins Street, now a community center. It is on the National Register.

heritage.architect: Willis R. Biggers (NRIS also lists Dudley and Carlton)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Plant City High School)

heritage.story: Tampa architect Willis R. Biggers designed the original Plant City High School, built in 1914 at 605 North Collins Street. The high school later moved to a new building completed in 1972, and the 1914 building became a community center. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 4, 1981.
heritage.visiting: A community center on North Collins Street; the city history page says the East Hillsborough Historical Society is on its first floor.

notes: Conflict to check: the city's history page places the East Hillsborough Historical Society (2,000+ books and files) on the first floor of this building, but Visit Tampa Bay's listing for the Plant City History and Photo Archives says it is 'Now located at 110 East Reynolds St., Suite 90'. The record does not claim public hours. Verifier (2026-09-27): Nominatim's OSM address point for 605 N Collins St (28.019168, -82.124002) matches the Census point; Wikipedia's coordinate is about 270 m west, so the Census point is kept. The Plant City History & Photo Archives (plantcityhistory.org) is a separate organization now at 110 E Reynolds St; that does not contradict the city's statement about the East Hillsborough Historical Society, which was not re-confirmed.

name: African American Heritage Trail
aliases: St. Pete African American Heritage Trail
address: Starts at the Carter G. Woodson African American Museum, 2240 9th Ave S
summary: A self-guided walking tour of 19 markers in two corridors, 22nd Street South and 9th Avenue South, on the history of St. Petersburg's African American community. Both routes start at the Carter G. Woodson African American Museum.

heritage.story: The city says John and Anna Donaldson, the first African American settlers on the Pinellas peninsula, arrived in 1868. Under Jim Crow laws Black residents built their own commercial, professional and entertainment street along 22nd Street South; the 1931 City Charter set separate residential districts by race. The 22nd Street trail covers businesses, the Manhattan Casino, the 1948 Royal Theater and Mercy Hospital (opened 1923); the 9th Avenue trail covers churches, Jordan Elementary School, the Fannye Ayer Ponder Council House and the Jordan Park housing complex, which opened in 1941 with 446 apartments.
heritage.visiting: Each corridor is about 1.25 miles with ten stops. Groups and classes can arrange a guided walking or trolley tour through the African American Heritage Association, per the city.

notes: Point is the trail start (Woodson museum, 2240 9th Ave S). The heritage trail's own site (afamheritagestpete.com) did not respond (connection reset / HTTP 503) on Sep 27, 2026. The city page says 'nineteen markers' and also 'ten trail stops' per corridor; both are reported as the city states them.

name: Al Lang Stadium
summary: City-owned stadium on the downtown St. Petersburg waterfront, home of the Tampa Bay Rowdies (USL Championship soccer) since 2011. Built in 1947 as a baseball park, it hosted spring training and minor league baseball until 2008.
quote: Located directly on the waterfront of downtown St. Petersburg, Al Lang Stadium boasts one of the most picturesque backsdrops of any soccer venue throughout North America.

heritage.story: St. Petersburg built Waterfront Park on the site in 1923, where the Yankees and Cardinals trained. After World War II the city replaced it with Al Lang Stadium, named for former mayor Al Lang, who promoted the city for spring training. The ballpark hosted spring training and minor league baseball until 2008; the Rowdies moved in for the 2011 season and converted it for soccer.
heritage.visiting: Open for Rowdies matches and other events.

notes: Rowdies page: home since 2011; built 1947; named for Mayor Al Lang; Waterfront Park 1923 on the site; 1976 renovation to 7,227 seats; baseball until 2008; club took managing control of the city-owned stadium in late 2014. name: American Victory Ship and Mariners Memorial Museum
hours_text: Monday noon–5 PM; Tuesday–Sunday 10 AM–5 PM.
price_text: Adults $15; seniors, veterans and college students $12; youth (4–17) $10; children 3 and under free.
summary: A World War II cargo ship moored next to the Florida Aquarium that you can tour as a museum. The 455-foot SS American Victory was delivered in 1945 and later served in the Korean and Vietnam wars; it arrived in Tampa in 1999.
quote: 1 of only 3 fully-operational Victory Class WWII ships remaining

heritage.story: The SS American Victory was built in 55 days at the California Shipbuilding yard in Los Angeles and delivered to the U.S. War Shipping Administration on May 24, 1945. She carried military cargo in the Korean War (from 1951) and the Vietnam War (from 1966). She arrived in Tampa, her new home port, on September 16, 1999, and after four years of volunteer restoration sailed on a shakedown cruise with 497 passengers and crew on September 20, 2003. The museum says the ship is on the National Register of Historic Places.
heritage.visiting: The ship is open to visitors during museum hours.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

name: Anclote Key Lighthouse
hours_text: Open for climbing the second weekend of each month (Friday–Sunday), 10 a.m.–4 p.m., October–May; next open house Oct. 9–11, 2026. Visitors can walk up to the locked fence any day from dawn to dusk.
price_text: A 7-dollar donation per person is requested for climbing
summary: An 1887 cast-iron skeletal lighthouse on the southern end of Anclote Key, three miles off Tarpon Springs, relit in 2003 inside Anclote Key Preserve State Park. Volunteers open it for climbing on monthly open-house weekends from October to May; the island is reached only by boat.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Anclote Keys Light)

heritage.story: The lighthouse was built in 1887 on Anclote Key, the largest of the Anclote Keys. After it was automated in 1952 the tower and other buildings were often vandalized, and the Coast Guard deactivated the light in 1984; the site passed to the State of Florida and became part of Anclote Key Preserve State Park. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1999 and, by 2003, had been restored and relit with a reproduction fourth-order Fresnel lens.
heritage.visiting: Reached only by private boat or ferry: the state park lists Island Paradise Charters and Parrotdise Express, and Odyssey Cruises from the Sponge Docks. The Friends of Anclote Key open the tower for climbing the second weekend of each month, October to May, and run private tours; on other days the tower is seen from its locked fence.

summary: An 1888 Carpenter Gothic church built by Dunedin's pioneer families, saved and moved to Hammock Park by the Dunedin Historical Society. The Dunedin History Museum runs it for weddings and community events.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Built in 1888 as Andrews Memorial Church at Scotland Street and Highland Avenue, the building was renamed Andrews Memorial Chapel and moved in 1926 to make way for what is now the First Presbyterian Church of Dunedin. The Dunedin Historical Society bought it in 1970 to save it from demolition, cut it in half and moved it to Hammock Park, where restoration began in 1974. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on July 31, 1972.
heritage.visiting: Next to Hammock Park. The Dunedin History Museum operates the chapel for weddings, christenings, memorials and community events; contact the chapel manager for access.

name: 1937 Antifascist Women's March marker and mural
summary: A 2023 marker and a 'No pasarán' mural on 7th Avenue recalling May 6, 1937, when thousands of Ybor City Latinas marched to City Hall against fascism in Spain.

heritage.story: On May 6, 1937, some 5,000 Latinas from Ybor City gathered on 7th Avenue and marched to downtown Tampa to present Mayor R. E. L. Chancey with a petition supporting Spain's Republic. During the Spanish Civil War the community sent food, clothing, 20,000 cigars, four ambulances, an X-ray machine and medicine to Republican forces, and 24 Ybor men joined the Abraham Lincoln Brigade. Michelle Sawyer's mural shows Dolores Ibárruri, Luisa Moreno and Margot Falcón Blanco.
heritage.visiting: The marker stands in front of the Ybor City Development Corporation building; the mural is on its west wall.

name: Babe Zaharias Golf Course
summary: A public golf course laid out in 1925, bought in 1949 by Babe Didrikson Zaharias and her husband George, and reopened by the City of Tampa in 1974 under her name. It is managed by the Tampa Sports Authority.
quote: Known in the Tampa Bay area as "The Babe," Babe Zaharias Golf Course was named after Mildred Ella "Babe" Didrikson Zaharias

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Designed in 1925 by J. Franklin Meehan for Burks L. Hamner's Forest Hills development, the course opened as the Northside Country Club and was soon renamed Forest Hills. George Zaharias bought it in 1949, and he and Babe, an Olympic champion and co-founder of the LPGA, ran it until 1955, when they moved to Texas after her cancer diagnosis. The City of Tampa took it over and reopened it in 1974 as the Babe Zaharias Golf Course; a county historical marker was added in 2023.
heritage.visiting: Public golf; book tee times through the Tampa Sports Authority. The historical marker is on the course grounds.

notes: The developer is spelled 'Burks L. Hammer' on the marker and 'B.L. Hamner' in the City book.

name: Balbin Brothers Cigar Factory
summary: A 1904 brick cigar factory built for the Samuel I. Davis Company and occupied by the Balbin Brothers from 1911 through the 1930s; West Tampa still calls it the Balbin Brothers building.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
West Tampa Historic District (National Register)

heritage.story: Like most cigar factories of its time, the building pairs a practical plan with a facade in a popular style. Cigar makers often moved from building to building while making the same label; this one was built for the Samuel I. Davis Company, and the Balbin Brothers used it from 1911 through the 1930s.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only.

heritage.story: Senator John S. Taylor built the Capitol Theatre, which opened on March 21, 1921, with the silent film Dinty and 944 seats. For seven decades it presented vaudeville, cultural events and movies. Facing foreclosure in 2009, it was bought by the City of Clearwater, which partnered with Ruth Eckerd Hall to run it; a 2013 renovation expanded it into neighboring buildings, and it was renamed for donors Nancy and David Bilheimer in 2019.

heritage.style: Beaux Arts characteristics (NHL nomination); the club calls it Renaissance Mediterranean

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: In 1902 a group of 546 immigrants from Asturias founded the club as a branch of the Centro Asturiano de La Habana; membership brought hospital, cemetery and health benefits. After fire destroyed its earlier clubhouse at Palm and Nebraska, members built the present three-story yellow brick and stone building for $110,000. Its theater, which the NHL nomination counts at 1,062 seats, drew zarzuela companies and performers such as Ernesto Lecuona. The NHL nomination notes that the building has never been vacant.
heritage.visiting: Free history tours every Tuesday at 10 a.m. (about one hour; sign up online). The club says the tour covers the building's history, not its event spaces; venue tours are by phone.

name: Cespedes Hall historical marker
address: N Albany Ave near W Main St
summary: A 2024 marker for Cespedes Hall, the wooden hall (1895–1898) that housed West Tampa's government offices and was a base for Cubans supporting the war for independence from Spain. The building is gone; the marker stands near Albany Avenue and Main Street.

heritage.story: La Sociedad Patriótica Céspedes de West Tampa paid $20,000 to build the hall, which also held a school, West Tampa's government offices, an opera hall and businesses. West Tampa's first mayor, Fernando Figueredo Socarrás, named it for his mentor Carlos Manuel de Céspedes, hero of Cuba's Ten Years' War, and it became a rallying point for workers who gave money and time to the 1895 independence war. The City of West Tampa demolished the wooden building in late 1898, likely for fear of fire.
heritage.visiting: The marker is on North Albany Avenue near Main Street.

notes: Erected in 2024 by the Hillsborough County Historical Advisory Council. The point is the Albany/Main intersection.

name: Chinsegut Hill Historic Site
hours_text: Weekend tours start at 10 a.m., noon and 2 p.m. every Saturday and Sunday
summary: A historic manor house on one of the highest points in Florida, near Brooksville, set in a 114-acre preserve and shown on docent-led weekend tours by the Tampa Bay History Center. Its story runs from an enslaver's plantation before the Civil War to the Robins family's progressive-era guests, including Thomas Edison and Helen Keller.
quote: Chinsegut Hill has witnessed thousands of years of Florida’s history.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Chinsegut Hill Manor House)

heritage.story: In the 1840s Bird Pearson brought his family and enslaved people to a Hernando County homestead and set up a plantation; the Ederington family bought it in 1852 and built the first version of the current house. The Robins family restored the house from 1904, named it Chinsegut Hill and entertained Thomas Edison, J.C. Penney and Helen Keller. In 1932 Raymond and Margaret Robins deeded more than 2,000 acres to the federal government for $1; the University of Florida later held the property and the University of South Florida leased it from 1958 to 2008. Since 2019 the Tampa Bay History Center has run weekend tours with Hernando County.
heritage.visiting: Docent-led tours on Saturdays and Sundays at 10 a.m., noon and 2 p.m.; tickets are sold through the Tampa Bay History Center.

heritage.story: In January 1824 Col. George Mercer Brooke arrived in Tampa Bay with four companies of infantry under orders to establish a military post; the fort served as a garrison for the Seminole Wars, and the village of Tampa grew up beside it. The park's stainless steel and bronze cenotaph by Bob Haozous honors the dead whose remains lie elsewhere.
heritage.visiting: Open 7 AM–10 PM; next to the Tampa Bay History Center, with an overlook, a canoe launch and boat slips (72-hour limit).

summary: A National Park Service site where the Manatee River meets Tampa Bay that commemorates Hernando de Soto's 1539 landing and expedition. It has a monument, a coastal nature trail and ranger programs.

heritage.story: In May 1539 Hernando de Soto's army of soldiers, hired mercenaries, craftsmen and clergy made landfall in Tampa Bay and met fierce resistance from Indigenous people defending their homelands; the expedition became a four-year, 4,000-mile march across the Southeast. Congress authorized the memorial on March 11, 1948, and it was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1966. The National Register inventory notes that historians do not agree this was the actual landing site.
heritage.visiting: Walk the grounds and the nature trail; Wikipedia gives 3,000 feet of shoreline. The park's home page lists ranger-led kayak tours, living history at Camp Uzita and an escape room booked through Recreation.gov.

name: Egmont Key State Park
hours_text: Daily, 8 a.m. to sunset, 365 days a year.
price_text: No park fee; ferry or boat fare applies (Hubbard's Marina ferry from Fort De Soto: $45 ages 12 and up, $25 ages 3-11).
summary: An island state park and wildlife refuge at the mouth of Tampa Bay, southwest of Fort De Soto, reached only by boat. Visitors walk about 6 miles of brick paths through the ruins of Fort Dade (1898-1923) past the 1858 lighthouse, and swim, snorkel, fish and collect shells; the south end is a closed shorebird refuge. There is no drinking water, restroom or store, and pets are not allowed.
quote: Accessible only by boat, Egmont Key has a unique natural and cultural history, including a lighthouse that has stood since 1858.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Egmont Key)

heritage.story: The lighthouse that stands today replaced an earlier light in 1858 and is maintained by the U.S. Coast Guard. At the end of the Third Seminole War the island held a camp for captured Seminoles, and Union forces occupied it during the Civil War. Fort Dade was built in 1898 for the Spanish–American War and housed 300 residents; Egmont Key stayed a military reservation until 1923. The Egmont Key Alliance says the island has lost more than half its land since 1898 to storms and rising seas, and that in 2024 Hurricanes Helene and Milton pushed surge 15 feet up the lighthouse and closed the island for more than six months.
heritage.visiting: Reached only by boat; ferries run from Fort De Soto. Since August 2026 the state park says all structures remain closed to the public, so the lighthouse and the Fort Dade ruins are seen from outside; the south end and part of the east beach are closed year-round for nesting birds.

status_note: Open, boat access only. Hubbard's Marina runs the ferry from the Fort De Soto boat ramp daily at 9 and 11 a.m., plus 2 p.m. on Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday (ferry page, read Sep 27, 2026). The Egmont Key Alliance says the island stayed closed for 6+ months after Hurricanes Helene and Milton in 2024.

heritage.style: Mediterranean Revival (French Renaissance Revival with Moorish and Spanish influences)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
National Historic Landmark
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: El Centro Español, incorporated in December 1891, was the first ethnic club in Ybor City; by 1908 it had 2,687 members, and the NHL nomination calls its 1906 Sanatorio probably the most modern hospital in Florida at the time. The club put up this dark red brick building in 1912 with a cantina, theater and ballroom, and sold it in 1983. After years of vacancy the building was restored, and Centro Ybor opened around it in 2000. The society still exists as a heritage organization.
heritage.visiting: The building is part of Centro Ybor on 7th Avenue (shops, restaurants, entertainment); the Ybor City Visitor Information Center is in the same complex at 1600 E 8th Ave, Suite B104.

heritage.story: Built as an ethnic club for the immigrants of the City of West Tampa, El Centro Español offered low-cost family medical care, education, recreation, entertainment and citizenship programs. Wikipedia reports that the building stood empty for years, was restored by the City of Tampa, served as a temporary home for the Tampa Museum of Art, and was leased in 2010 to the Hillsborough Education Foundation.

heritage.story: The NHL nomination says Vicente Martínez-Ybor and Eduardo Manrara erected the building in 1895 to house the Cherokee Club, which accepted both Latin and American members and offered rooms to members and guests including Grover Cleveland, Gen. Leonard Wood and the artist Frederick Remington. When completed it was only the second brick building in Ybor City. Its arcade of 38 arched brick columns lines the ground floor, and a restoration was completed in 1988.

summary: A 20-room Mediterranean-style winter house built in the early 1930s for Bethlehem Steel executive Charles Austin Buck, with gardens by the Olmsted firm, inside Bok Tower Gardens. It is on the National Register and is seen on docent-led tours.

heritage.architect: Charles R. Wait (house); William Lyman Phillips of the Olmsted firm (gardens)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Charles Austin Buck, a Bethlehem Steel vice president, hired the Olmsted firm to design his winter estate next to Mountain Lake; William Lyman Phillips began the gardens in 1929, and architect Charles Wait was engaged in 1930 to design the 12,900-square-foot house with barrel-tile roofs, carved doors and wrought iron. The family used it six to twelve weeks a year. In 1970 an effort led by Nellie Lee Holt Bok, daughter-in-law of Edward W. Bok, brought the home into Bok Tower Gardens, and landscape architect Rudy Favretti restored it with volunteers. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.
heritage.visiting: Buy the tour at the Entrance Gate or Visitor Center before walking to the house. Stairs lead to the second floor and there is no elevator; food and drink are not allowed inside.

heritage.story: College president Ludd Spivey asked Frank Lloyd Wright to design a new campus in 1938, and Wright first walked the grounds, a citrus-covered hill above Lake Hollingsworth, on May 8, 1938, envisioning buildings growing 'out of the ground and into the light – a Child of the Sun.' Over more than 20 years he delivered 18 designs, and 13 were built, beginning with the Annie Pfeiffer Chapel (1938–1941); students supplied labor for the first five, and during World War II the crew was almost entirely women. The buildings are linked by more than a mile of covered walkways, the Esplanade. The campus was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2012.
heritage.visiting: A 90-minute Basic Campus Tour visits the Pfeiffer Chapel, the E. T. Roux Library and the Usonian Faculty House; a 2.5-hour In-depth Tour adds Danforth Chapel, the Ordway Arts Building and the Polk County Science Building with Wright's only planetarium. Tickets are sold at the GEICO Gift Shop, 840 Johnson Avenue.

summary: The Spanish–American War coastal fort on Mullet Key that gave Fort De Soto Park its name, with its 12-inch mortar battery, brick roads and a small museum. The battery is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Fort Desoto Batteries)

heritage.story: Mullet Key was declared a military reservation in 1849 after an Army engineers' survey. Construction of Fort De Soto, a subpost of Fort Dade on Egmont Key, began in November 1898 and was completed in 1906; Battery Laidley held eight 12-inch coast defense mortars and Battery Bigelow two 3-inch guns, to protect Tampa Bay, and the fort was active until 1910. Pinellas County bought the land in 1938, sold it back to the federal government in 1941 for a World War II gunnery and bombing range, and repurchased it in 1948. The 12-inch mortar battery was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1977.
heritage.visiting: Inside Fort De Soto Park: the battery with its remaining 12-inch mortars, two British rapid-fire rifles of 1890 vintage installed in 1982, markers where the post's buildings stood, and the Quartermaster Storehouse Museum. designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Lieutenant Colonel William S. Foster arrived with 430 men on December 1, 1836, and within weeks had built two blockhouses, a large storehouse and a fort to guard the Hillsborough River crossing. The post was abandoned and reactivated several times through the Second Seminole War and was used only for short periods as late as 1849. The fort standing today is a reconstruction that the state built on the site and opened to the public in February 1980; the site was listed on the National Register in 1972.
heritage.visiting: Guided tours only (third Saturdays, November to April), plus living-history events such as Fort Foster Days (February 13–14, 2027). Artifacts from the site are in the Interpretive Center inside Hillsborough River State Park.

name: Fortune Taylor Bridge (Laurel Street Bridge)

summary: A 1927 drawbridge over the Hillsborough River, renamed in 2017 for Fortune Taylor, a formerly enslaved woman whose homestead land on the east bank became Fortune Street. A 2018 marker at the west end tells her story.

designations.name: City of Tampa multiple property designation: Historic Bridges on the Hillsborough River

heritage.story: Fortune and Benjamin Taylor married as free people in Tampa on May 5, 1866, and Benjamin claimed a 33-acre homestead on the east side of the river, where they grew oranges, guavas and peaches; after his death Fortune was granted the homestead in 1875. The street through the property was named for her, and the first Fortune Street Bridge, financed by Hugh C. Macfarlane, was built in 1892 to help West Tampa's cigar industry. A tugboat knocked that bridge off its foundation in 1901; the present drawbridge was begun in 1924, completed in 1927, and renamed the Fortune Taylor Bridge in 2017. Fortune Taylor died in 1906 and is buried in Oaklawn Cemetery.
heritage.visiting: The marker is at West Laurel Street and Doyle Carlton Drive, on the right when traveling west on Laurel Street.

summary: The tabby mansion of Robert Gamble's sugar plantation on the Manatee River, worked by enslaved people, later donated to the state as a Confederate memorial. It is a state park seen on guided tours.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Benjamin, Judah P., Memorial / Robert Gamble House)

heritage.story: Major Robert Gamble built the mansion between about 1845 and 1850 as the center of a sugar plantation that at its height covered 3,500 acres; he likely enslaved more than 200 people to work the land and process the cane. Its columns and two-foot-thick walls are tabby, a mix used in place of brick. Confederate cabinet officer Judah P. Benjamin stayed there in May 1865 while fleeing Union forces. In 1925 the United Daughters of the Confederacy bought the house and grounds and gave them to the state as a memorial to Benjamin; the mansion was listed in the National Register in 1970, and the state added the ruins of the sugar mill to the park in 2002.
heritage.visiting: The mansion is seen on guided tours, six a day Thursday through Monday; the grounds include a 40,000-gallon cistern and the 1872 Patten House, and the fenced ruins of the sugar mill are half a mile north on State Road 683.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
National Historic Landmark

heritage.story: Railroad and steamship owner Henry B. Plant built the Tampa Bay Hotel as a winter resort; it operated from 1891 to 1932. During the Spanish-American War of 1898 it served as a military headquarters, and Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders were stationed on its grounds. Since 1933 the building has housed the University of Tampa and the museum, which took the name Henry B. Plant Museum in 1974.
heritage.visiting: The museum occupies part of Plant Hall on the University of Tampa campus; the rest of the building is university space.

accessibility: Ramps at the north end and west side of the building; a free wheelchair (first come, first served); a free self-guided audio tour in English and Spanish with large-print transcripts; White Glove Tours for visitors who are blind or partially sighted (two weeks' notice).

name: Hillsborough River State Park
hours_text: Daily, 8 a.m. to sunset, 365 days a year.
price_text: $6 per vehicle.
summary: A state park near Thonotosassa where the Hillsborough River runs over Class II rapids, which the park notes are rare in Florida; it has four hiking trails totaling about 7.3 miles, canoe, kayak and bike rentals, a 112-site campground, picnic pavilions built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, and the interpretive center for Fort Foster State Historic Site.
quote: Besides enjoying a living history lesson, visitors can view Class II river rapids, which are rare in Florida, and canoe or kayak along the scenic Hillsborough River.

heritage.story: Hillsborough River State Park was one of the eight original Florida state parks created in 1938 and was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps; CCC buildings, the suspension bridge and a section of fence survive, and visitors still picnic under CCC pavilions from the 1930s. The park also holds a replica of Fort Foster, which was garrisoned on and off from December 1836 to April 1838 during the Second Seminole War to defend the river crossing.
heritage.visiting: The park's interpretive center serves Fort Foster State Historic Site; Wikipedia says the fort replica can be seen only on weekend tours.

status_note: Open, with some areas still closed: the park reopened Feb. 24, 2025 after the 2024 storms, but the cafe, recreation hall, several campsites, two pavilions, the Seminole Trail and parts of the Rapids Trail remain closed. From Aug. 4, 2026 canoe, kayak and bike rentals run Monday and Thursday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Friday to Sunday 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., closed Tuesday and Wednesday (state park page, read Sep 27, 2026).

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Pasco County Courthouse)

heritage.story: Dade City was incorporated in 1889 and is the county seat of Pasco County. Its centerpiece is the Pasco County Courthouse, built in 1909 to a design by Georgia architect Edward Columbus Hosford and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2006. The city's historic register lists more than 150 properties, among them the former Atlantic Coast Line depot, now the Dade City Heritage and Cultural Museum.
heritage.visiting: Walk the downtown streets and the self-guided historic walking tour (the courthouse is stop No. 1); the city publishes walking tour guides and a map of historic properties.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Munn Park Historic District)

heritage.story: The Munn Park Historic District, named for Lakeland founder Abraham Munn, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on November 3, 1997, with 48 historic buildings around the central Munn Park. Its downtown commercial district, bounded by Baker and Wheeler Streets and the railroad tracks, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 8, 1993, with 38 historic buildings. The 1909 Union Depot downtown is now the Robert W. Willaford Railroad Museum.

name: Historic Kenwood
summary: A National Register district of bungalows just north of St. Petersburg's Grand Central District, developed from 1912. The neighborhood association calls it St. Pete's first suburb.
quote: Kenwood was St. Pete’s first suburb and its first neighborhood for year-round residents

heritage.style: Bungalow/Craftsman (NRIS); frame and masonry vernacular, Tudor, Mediterranean and Colonial Revival also present

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Kenwood Historic District)

heritage.story: In 1912 Philadelphia developer Charles Hall bought 160 acres of avocado groves about two miles northwest of downtown and began selling building lots; his first model home, built in 1918, is now the Craftsman House Gallery. Most homes were built between the 1920s and the 1950s, and 170 were moved here from other neighborhoods in the 1930s. The district, with 2,203 historic buildings, was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2003; St. Petersburg High School (1926) stands in it on 5th Avenue North. Wikipedia notes that urban pioneers began reviving Kenwood and the Grand Central District in the early 1990s and that the LGBT community played a notable role in the revitalization.
heritage.visiting: A residential neighborhood; walk its brick avenues and hexagon-paver sidewalks among bungalows. Several sections are also city local historic districts.

notes: Wikipedia says homes were built 1912–1945; the association says 1920s–1950s; the association wording is used. Point is the OSM neighbourhood node. heritage.story: The North Shore Historic District, commonly known as Old Northeast or Historic Old Northeast, is bounded by 4th Street North, 5th Avenue North, Tampa Bay and 30th Avenue North. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 20, 2003, with 2,975 historic buildings. The National Park Service record gives its periods of significance as 1900 to 1949 and its main styles as Bungalow/Craftsman and Colonial Revival.

name: Historic Spanish Point
aliases: Selby Gardens Historic Spanish Point campus
hours_text: Outdoor areas open daily 10 a.m.–5 p.m.; White Cottage, Mary's Chapel, Window to the Past and Packing House 10:30 a.m.–4:30 p.m.; Guptill House 10 a.m.–4 p.m. when a volunteer docent is available
price_text: Adults $20; ages 5-17 $12; ages 4 and under free; Selby members free
summary: Marie Selby Botanical Gardens' 30-acre campus on Little Sarasota Bay in Osprey, where you walk among prehistoric shell middens and a burial mound, the Webb family's pioneer homestead buildings and chapel, and the gardens of Bertha Palmer's early-1900s Osprey Point estate.
quote: visitors can explore ancient peoples, pioneer history, the Palmer Legacy, and native plants.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Osprey Archeological and Historic Site)

heritage.story: The site holds an archaeological record of about 5,000 years of Florida prehistory, including a shell midden and a burial mound built from about 300 to 1000. The Webb family from Utica, New York, homesteaded here and named it Spanish Point after advice from a Spanish trader; in 1910 Chicago socialite Bertha Palmer bought it for her Osprey Point estate and kept the pioneer buildings. In 1975 it became the first site in Sarasota County listed on the National Register, and in May 2020 it became a campus of Marie Selby Botanical Gardens.
heritage.visiting: Walk the grounds daily; several historic buildings have shorter hours, and the Bayside Cottage Café is open 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.

notes: Prices from the campus visit page (read with WebFetch 2026-09-27). Selby Gardens' downtown campus belongs to the outdoors slice; this record is only the Osprey campus. Wikipedia gives the older street number 337 N Tamiami Trail and 33 acres; Selby's page gives 401 and 30 acres.

When it needed more room, Peter O. Knight donated the land for this building and a tree-filled park. The City of Tampa says it became the largest publicly supported home for the elderly in Tampa.

name: Huggins-Stengel Field
summary: A baseball field in Crescent Lake Park built in 1925 for New York Yankees spring training and later used by the Mets and Orioles. It is on the National Register and is a city landmark.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: The field in Crescent Lake Park was built in 1925 as the New York Yankees' spring training practice field under manager Miller Huggins, and was renamed Miller Huggins Field in 1931. Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Joe DiMaggio trained here, and later Casey Stengel's Yankees; after Stengel took over the new New York Mets, the Mets trained here and the field was renamed Huggins-Stengel Field in 1963. The Baltimore Orioles used it from 1992 to 1995. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2019.
heritage.visiting: In Crescent Lake Park; two bronze plaques honor Miller Huggins and Casey Stengel. The field now hosts high school and college games, per Wikipedia.

name: Hyde Park Historic District
summary: About 600 acres of late 19th- and early 20th-century revival-style houses and bungalows on tree-lined streets between the Hillsborough River, the bay and Howard Avenue. It is a National Register and City of Tampa historic district.

heritage.style: Late Victorian, revival styles and bungalows

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic district

heritage.story: O. H. Platt bought 20 acres of the Robert Jackson homestead in 1886 and subdivided it into residential lots; after the Tampa Bay Hotel opened in 1891, Hyde Park drew prominent residents. The first bridge over the Hillsborough River, the Lafayette Street Bridge of 1888, linked it to the City of Tampa. The local district, expanded in 2023, counts 918 contributing buildings, including schools, churches and commercial buildings as well as houses.
heritage.visiting: Walk the streets west of the University of Tampa toward Hyde Park Village and Bayshore Boulevard; the houses are private.

name: Jackson Rooming House
summary: A two-story boarding house a block from Union Station that lodged Black travelers, railroad workers and touring musicians during segregation. The City says it is the only such boarding house left standing in Tampa; a foundation is working to stabilize and restore it.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Moses and Sarah Jackson built the house as their residence (the foundation says 1901; the City dates Moses Jackson's purchase to 1899) and expanded it into a boarding house near Tampa Union Station, which opened in 1912. Because African Americans were barred from white hotels until the early 1960s, it housed Black railroad workers, servicemen and entertainers; the foundation lists guests including Count Basie, Cab Calloway, Ella Fitzgerald, James Brown and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The family ran it as a boarding house into the 1990s.
heritage.visiting: Not open to the public; see the exterior and the Soulwalk marker in front of the house.

notes: End of boarding use: the City's Soulwalk page says the 1990s; Wikipedia says 1989. Wikipedia (citing news reports) describes stalled restoration and a 2023 City Council land-swap vote with a neighboring parking owner; status as of Sep 2026 not confirmed on the foundation site, which asks for help to 'Stabilize and Restore' the house.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: The Tocobaga inhabited the site for about 600 years, from roughly 1000 to 1600 CE, in a village complex whose mounds once stretched more than 3 miles along Boca Ciega Bay; most were removed for fill during 20th-century development. The remaining mounds include a 12-foot plaza mound and a long midden mound running from the city park onto private property. The site is identified with the landing of the Narváez expedition, and the Diocese of St. Petersburg placed a marker there for what it calls the first Catholic Mass in Florida. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 4, 2003.
heritage.visiting: The public part is the city's Jungle Prada de Narvaez park, with picnic tables, a fishing pier and a boat launch; the better-preserved mounds are on private land.

summary: The 1892 Victorian house in Bartow built by Lawrence B. Brown, a formerly enslaved self-taught carpenter who became a successful builder and property owner. The nine-room house is a museum shown on free guided tours by appointment, and an L.B. Brown Heritage Festival is held each February.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Lawrence B. Brown was born into slavery in Alachua County; after emancipation his family moved to Volusia County, where he taught himself carpentry and built homes to rent or sell. He later moved to Bartow during an economic boom and kept building, including this nine-room, 1,700-square-foot Victorian house in 1892. The house is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
heritage.visiting: Free docent tours by appointment on weekdays (weekends possible with several days' notice); the exterior can be seen any time.

summary: An Ybor City bakery founded in 1915 by Juan Moré that bakes Cuban bread by hand, laying a palmetto leaf across each loaf, and trucks it to restaurants and markets; its counter sells café con leche, Cuban toast, pastries and sandwiches. The family now runs four shops (Ybor, Kennedy Boulevard, Seminole Heights and St. Petersburg).
quote: One of our most important time-honored customs is placing a freshly cut palmetto leaf across the top of each loaf to create the signature split down the middle.

heritage.story: Juan Moré, a Catalan who had fought in the Spanish-American War in Cuba, joined a co-op of bakers and cigar makers around the start of World War I that opened three Ybor City bakeries: La Primera, La Segunda and La Tercera. When the other two folded, he bought La Segunda from his partners. The bakery says it is run by the fourth generation of the family and bakes about 20,000 loaves a day.
heritage.visiting: The Ybor City bakery counter is open 6:30 AM–3 PM daily.

heritage.story: Segregation split the Club Nacional Cubano, which had served Black and white Cubans, into the Círculo Cubano and Los Libres Pensadores Martí-Maceo, whose first official meeting took place on October 26, 1900, at the home of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso; it later merged with La Unión, an Afro-Cuban society in West Tampa. Its clubhouse at 1907–1909 E. 6th Avenue was demolished in 1965 during urban renewal. The society moved into this converted commercial building, which has a tile panel celebrating its namesakes; the NHL nomination classes it as contributing to the district because of its exceptional importance.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Madira Bickel Mounds)

heritage.story: In 1974 women of Manatee United Methodist Church set out to save the congregation's 1887 sanctuary and Manatee County's first courthouse (1860), both slated for demolition. The two buildings were moved to the site in December 1975, and the park opened on July 4, 1976. It has since grown to fourteen structures, including the 1903 Wiggins General Store, the Fogarty Boat Works and the 1908 Bunker Hill schoolhouse.

name: Historic Manhattan Casino
hours_text: Office Monday–Friday 9 am–4 pm; tours by appointment
summary: A 1925 dance hall on 22nd Street South that was the center of Black St. Petersburg's entertainment during segregation. Restored and reopened, it is rented for events and can be toured by appointment.
quote: Founded in 1925, the Manhattan Casino stands as a beacon of cultural significance in St. Petersburg’s history.

designations.name: St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: In 1925 African American entrepreneur Elder Jordan Sr. contracted with R. L. Sharpe to build a 12,000-square-foot, two-story entertainment hall on 22nd Street South; the city says it first opened as the Jordan Dance Hall in 1931 and later became the Manhattan Casino. It was part of 'The Deuces,' the business and entertainment hub of the African American community in segregation-era St. Pete, and a stop on the Chitlin' Circuit. Performers included Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Cab Calloway, Ray Charles, Nat King Cole, Fats Domino and James Brown. It closed in 1968 and the city designated it a local landmark in 1994.
heritage.visiting: Tours by appointment through the venue; its Jordan Ballroom and Legacy Room are rented for events. It is a stop on the city's African American Heritage Trail.

notes: The official site (copyright City of St. Petersburg, contact manhattancasino@stpete.org) says 'after careful restoration, we're proud to reopen our doors' and 'tours are available by appointment'. The city's attractions page says 'Built in 1925' and 'first opened as the Jordan Dance Hall in 1931'; the heritage trail page says it was 'constructed in 1925 by Elder Jordan Sr. ... and his sons'. The city attractions page phone is 727-892-5496; the venue site's main number 727-892-5400 is used. The Chitlin' Circuit and 'Elder Jordan Sr. and his sons' are on the city's heritage-trail page. heritage.story: Beginning in about 1912, Longboat Key developer Rufus Jordan built early houses on the north end of the key from rusticated stone blocks, and the Mar Vista building is one of them; it survived the 1921 hurricane. After 1947 the property became a fish camp with a pub, and in the 1950s it grew into a popular restaurant and bar. Chiles Hospitality bought it in the 1980s to keep its Old Florida feel, and Beachside Hospitality Group bought it in 2024.

Boza Sr. bought and turned into burial plots. The City purchased the Colón parcels in May 2023 and now owns both.

name: Masonic Temple No. 25 (Hillsborough Lodge No. 25)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Hillsborough Lodge No. 25 chose Elliott, one of its members, to design a building for ceremonial, administrative and commercial uses; its terra cotta ornament shows the gavel, plumb, ruler, square, level and trowel. The cornerstone of the lodge's fourth building was laid on June 18, 1928, and the first meeting in the new temple was held on February 19, 1929.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only, at the corner of Kennedy Boulevard and Morgan Street.

name: May-Stringer House (Hernando Heritage Museum)
hours_text: Tuesday–Saturday 11:00 AM–3:00 PM
summary: A four-story, seven-gable Victorian house in Brooksville that is now the Hernando Heritage Museum, with themed rooms such as a dining room, bedrooms, a military room, an 1880s doctor's office and a 1900s communication room, seen on guided tours. Hernando County's tourism office calls it one of Florida's top five haunted locations, and ghost tours run on weekends.
quote: The May-Stringer House is considered one of the top five haunted locations in Florida, and they offer ghost tours on weekends for those brave enough to experience it.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Richard Wiggins first homesteaded the land under the Armed Occupation Act; John L. May bought it in 1855 and built a four-room house for his family. Dr. Sheldon Stringer later added ten rooms, making the four-story, fourteen-room Victorian home that stands today. The Hernando Historical Museum Association runs it as a museum with more than 10,000 artifacts, and it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1997.
heritage.visiting: Guided tours Tuesday to Saturday; ghost tours on weekends.

name: Memorial Park Cemetery
address: 2425 E Dr Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
hours_text: 8 AM–6 PM daily.
summary: A 20-acre cemetery founded in 1919 for African American World War I veterans, which became the main burial ground for Tampa's Black community under segregation. The City of Tampa bought it in 2023.
quote: Established in 1919 for African American WWI veterans, this 20-acre cemetery became the primary burial ground for Tampa's Black community during the segregation era.

heritage.story: Segregation barred Black funerals from Tampa's growing number of private white cemeteries, and the city-owned cemeteries and the Black-owned Zion Cemetery were running out of room. After Memorial Park opened, Tampa's other Black cemeteries were acquired by white interests and their graves removed or built over; Memorial Park remained the only surviving Black cemetery until Zion and others were rediscovered in 2019 and 2020. The City began maintaining it in 2019 after its owner died and bought it in 2023; it holds nearly 20,000 known burials.
heritage.visiting: Open 8 AM–6 PM daily; the City takes requests to help locate a burial.

name: Mirror Lake Community Library
summary: St. Petersburg's Carnegie library, opened on Mirror Lake in 1915 and still a branch of the city library system. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (St. Petersburg Public Library)
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: The city won a 17,500 dollar grant from the Carnegie Corporation in 1913 and in 1914 chose a site on the banks of the city reservoir, now Mirror Lake. The Beaux-Arts library by Henry D. Whitfield opened in December 1915; the city calls it St. Petersburg's first library. The city refused Black residents access when it opened and began admitting them to the basement in 1944. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.

name: North Franklin Street Historic District
summary: A National Register district of early-20th-century commercial buildings at the north end of downtown's Franklin Street, the last surviving part of Tampa's early downtown business district.

heritage.style: Commercial styles of the early 20th century

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa multiple property designation: North Franklin Street / Downtown

heritage.story: The City of Tampa says these buildings are the last surviving elements of the early downtown business district, which began before 1900 and peaked in the 1930s, serving residents who lived between the Hillsborough River and Nebraska Avenue. The National Register district, listed on March 28, 2002, is bounded by Florida Avenue and East Fortune, Tampa, Franklin and East Harrison streets. The National Register nomination notes that the land boom slowed in 1926, when financial backing for the Davis Islands real estate venture collapsed.
heritage.visiting: Walk North Franklin Street between Harrison and Fortune streets; the buildings are private.

notes: The NRHP form counts 8 contributing buildings and a period of significance of c. 1903–c. 1921. City local designation years for the grouping span 2003–2017.

name: Oaklawn Cemetery
hours_text: 8 AM–6 PM daily.
summary: Tampa's first public burying ground, established in 1850 for 'white and slave, rich and poor', with the adjoining Catholic St. Louis Cemetery (1874). Tampa's first mayor and 12 other mayors, a Florida governor and Ybor City founder Vicente Martínez-Ybor are buried here.
quote: Tampa's first public cemetery (1850) represents every level of society, from enslaved people to governors.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The Alachua County Commission established Oaklawn as a public burying ground on April 1, 1850, when Tampa had about 500 people; a portion was set aside for enslaved people. In 1874 the Leonardi family donated adjoining land for the Catholic St. Louis Cemetery. Many early markers were carved cypress and were lost to fire, rot and storms, and the original plat was misplaced after the Civil War; the Sexton's House dates to 1910 and the receiving vault to 1894. The City lists about 1,700 known burials.
heritage.visiting: Open 8 AM–6 PM daily; the City publishes a self-guided walking tour of 20 stops. It asks visitors not to touch markers, make rubbings or step inside plot enclosures.

name: Old Courthouse Heritage Museum
hours_text: Museum: Tuesday–Saturday 10 a.m.–4 p.m.

summary: A free Citrus County history museum in the 1912 courthouse on the town square in downtown Inverness, with first-floor exhibits covering 12,000 years of local and Florida history and a restored second-floor courtroom, where Elvis Presley filmed a courtroom scene for "Follow That Dream" in 1961.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Citrus County Courthouse, Old)

heritage.story: Tampa architect Willis R. Biggers designed the courthouse, built in 1912, and it was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1992. The historical society says it draws on four architectural styles, two European and two American, and that it sits at a 45-degree angle on the downtown square so each of its four doorways faces a compass point. Today it is the Old Courthouse Heritage Museum, with exhibits on 12,000 years of Citrus County and Florida history.
heritage.visiting: Free; the first floor has exhibitions and the restored courtroom on the second floor is open to visitors. An elevator and ramp make it accessible, and there is free parking around the square.

heritage.architect: William Potter (1923 addition by M. Leo Elliott)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Hillsborough County High School, the county's earliest high school, opened here in 1911; a 1923 addition by M. Leo Elliott partly filled the building's open center. It later housed Thomas Jefferson Junior High (1928–1938) and Jefferson High School (until 1967), and in 2002 it was renamed the D. W. Waters Center for an educator who served as a principal for 41 years. It now specializes in career education.

name: 1860 Manatee County Courthouse

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Manatee County Courthouse, Original)

heritage.story: Manatee County was formed in 1855, and five years later the community built this small wood-framed courthouse; all government business for the county's 5,000 square miles took place in its courtroom. The building later belonged to the Manatee United Methodist congregation, and when it and the congregation's 1887 church were slated for demolition in 1974, the Manatee County Historical Commission moved both to the new museum in December 1975. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1976.
heritage.visiting: Seen at Manatee Village Historical Park, open Monday–Friday and the 2nd and 4th Saturdays, 9 AM–4 PM; admission is free.

notes: Separate record for the NRHP-listed 1860 courthouse inside around-daytrips' manatee-village-historical-park (whose record lists no designations); could instead be merged into it as a designation. Hours and admission read from manateevillage.org (via WebFetch). Verifier (2026-09-27): name changed to '1860 Manatee County Courthouse' (Manatee Village calls it the 1860 Courthouse; NRIS 'Manatee County Courthouse, Original') so it is not confused with the 1913 courthouse downtown; the old name is kept as an alias. Every claim re-checked on manateevillage.org.

name: Old Pinellas County Courthouse
summary: Pinellas County's Classical Revival courthouse in downtown Clearwater, designed by Francis J. Kennard, with its 1917 building and 1920s additions. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Pinellas County Courthouse, Old)

heritage.story: Designed by Francis J. Kennard, the courthouse replaced a hastily built structure that had been put up to help establish Clearwater as the county seat. The National Park Service record lists 1917, 1924 and 1926 as its significant years, for the original building and its additions. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on June 25, 1992.
heritage.visiting: Seen from Court Street in downtown Clearwater.

notes: Wikipedia's text says 'constructed in 1918' while its infobox and NRIS give 1917, 1924, 1926; NRIS used. Current use of the building (county offices) not confirmed on a county page; the record claims only the exterior.

name: Old School House
summary: A small school building from the 1850s, one of the oldest buildings in Tampa, later used by the Tampa Bay Hotel and cared for by the Daughters of the American Revolution since 1931. It stands on the University of Tampa campus.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The City of Tampa calls it the first freestanding, publicly accessible school house built in Hillsborough County; it was built as a school for girls, then served as an outbuilding of the Tampa Bay Hotel and later as a civic meeting space. In 1931 the DeSoto Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution asked Mayor McKay to save it, and the City gave it to the chapter on condition that it be restored and used as a meeting place and museum.
heritage.visiting: Wikipedia says it is open by appointment and during twice-yearly open houses.

notes: Wikipedia says it has been moved twice from its original site in what is now Plant Park.

name: Tampa City Hall (Old City Hall)
summary: Tampa's 1915 Beaux Arts city hall, whose clock tower made it a focal point of the early skyline. It still houses city government, including City Council offices on the third floor.

heritage.architect: B. C. Bonfoey and M. Leo Elliott (builder McGucken & Hyer)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Ground was broken in 1914, and the City of Tampa says the finished building was the tallest south of Jacksonville, with a tower that made it a focal point of the skyline. Its Seth Thomas clock is named for Hortense Oppenheimer, who led the effort to raise money for a public clock like those she had seen in northern cities. The building was documented by the Historic American Buildings Survey in 1981 and renovated in 2017.
heritage.visiting: A working government building; see the clock tower from Kennedy Boulevard and Florida Avenue.

notes: The OSM feature named 'Tampa City Hall' is the 306 E Jackson St building; the point here is the census match for 315 E Kennedy Blvd.

name: Old Tampa Free Public Library
summary: A Carnegie-funded Classical Revival library of 1915 designed by Fred J. James, Tampa's main library until 1968. It now holds library administrative offices; see it from the street.

heritage.architect: Fred J. James (builder Aulic, Bastes & Hudnell)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The City of Tampa says this was the second of two Tampa libraries built with Carnegie Foundation grants and that it served the public for more than 50 years. Wikipedia reports that construction was completed in 1915 but the library did not open until April 27, 1917, after a dispute over its operating budget, and that it was Tampa's main library until the new downtown library opened in 1968.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only; Wikipedia says the Tampa-Hillsborough County Public Library administration has occupied it since 2016.

notes: Wikipedia also says the building houses the City's Community Affairs Department in one passage and library administration in another; current tenant not confirmed on an official page.

name: Oldsmar Flea Market
hours_text: Saturday and Sunday 8am–3pm.
price_text: Free parking.
summary: Weekend flea market on 28 acres of mostly covered stalls on Race Track Road. Part of the property is being redeveloped as apartments, and the market is to keep operating on the remaining land (Tampa Bay Times, Jul 13, 2026).
quote: Welcome to the Oldsmar Flea Market where you can find just about anything. The market is a sprawling oasis of history and nostalgia spreading over 28 acres.
status_note: Plans filed in 2026 redevelop a large part of the site as the 279-unit Alton Oldsmar apartments; the market says it will stay open on the rest (Tampa Bay Times, Jul 13, 2026; Business Observer, Jul 15, 2026).
notes: Added by the verifier 2026-09-27. Site read with WebFetch and the r.jina.ai reader ('Our hours: Sat - Sun 8AM to 3 PM'; 'Dogs are welcome; however, they must be carried or in a stroller'). Point: OpenStreetMap feature on Race Track Road (Census match 140 m away); it sits by the county line near Tampa Bay Downs, which venues-bay also files under oldsmar.

name: Olivia
summary: A modern Italian restaurant on West Swann Avenue with a working dough room where the kitchen makes pizza dough, mozzarella, pasta and ravioli; a second location is in St. Petersburg. The 2026 MICHELIN Guide lists the Tampa restaurant as recommended.
quote: Watch as you dine while our team makes authentic Italian pizza dough, fresh mozzarella, pasta & ravioli in our working dough room.
notes: Michelin distinction read on Sep 27, 2026 from the MICHELIN Guide's own listing data (guide_year 2026, published 2026-05-28) behind guide.michelin.com (the HTML pages sit behind a bot challenge that WebFetch cannot pass) and cross-checked with visittampabay.com/michelin/, which lists the same 28 Tampa restaurants and distinctions. Page read rendered in a browser (SiteGround bot check).

name: O'Maddy's Bar and Grille
hours_text: Daily 11 AM–midnight (per Visit St. Pete-Clearwater)
summary: Bar and grill on the Gulfport waterfront with outdoor seating facing the water and the Gulfport pier, serving Gulf seafood, steaks, pasta and vegetarian dishes, with live music every day.
quote: Our outdoor seating offers great views of the Gulfport waterfront – watch the boats sail by, the fisherman on the Gulfport Pier, or the sun setting over the water.

name: Open Air Post Office
summary: St. Petersburg's 1916–1917 post office at First Avenue North and Fourth Street, known as the Open Air Post Office. It is on the National Register and was among the first city landmarks, designated in 1986.

heritage.architect: George W. Stewart; M. C. Holliday (per NRIS)
heritage.style: Classical Revival with Spanish Colonial elements

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: The federal post office at the southwest corner of First Avenue North and Fourth Street North was built in 1916 and 1917 and is known as the Open Air Post Office. The National Park Service record names George W. Stewart and M. C. Holliday as its architects. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on April 4, 1975, and designated a city landmark in 1986.
heritage.visiting: On the southwest corner of First Avenue North and Fourth Street North, downtown.

notes: Whether it still operates as a USPS retail counter was not confirmed on a readable page (the USPS locator is script-rendered); the record claims only the building.

name: The Orpheum
summary: Small live-music club that moved from Ybor City to North Nebraska Avenue in north Tampa, near the University of South Florida. It hosts live music and other events.
quote: The Orpheum has been showcasing live music and events for the better part of two decades.
notes: Official site: 'Formerly located in the Historic Ybor City entertainment district of Tampa, Florida. The Orpheum has now taken up residence in North Tampa. Minutes away from the University of South Florida.' Shows listed into mid-October 2026. The scope list placed it in Ybor; it is no longer there. Verifier 2026-09-27: homepage re-read; address, phone, quote verbatim, move from Ybor, shows listed Sep 27 - Oct 14, 2026.

name: Oscar Scherer State Park
hours_text: Daily, 8 a.m. to sunset, 365 days a year.
price_text: $5 per vehicle.
summary: A state park in Osprey between Sarasota and Venice that protects Florida scrub-jay habitat, with 15 miles of trails, the paved Legacy Trail running through it, swimming and fishing at three-acre Lake Osprey, paddling and fishing on South Creek, and a campground; bald eagles nest here in winter.
quote: A hidden gem surrounded by housing developments and major highways, Oscar Scherer plays an invaluable role in the preservation of Florida scrub-jay habitat.
notes: Verifier (2026-09-27): floridastateparks.org blocks curl and WebFetch, but its pages were read in full through the r.jina.ai reader; the record now rests on the park's own page. Opened in summer 1956 under the will of Elsa Scherer Burrows (Wikipedia).

name: Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church
summary: Ybor City's Catholic church, a buff brick Romanesque Revival building of 1937 that replaced a wooden church of 1891, which had served Catholics of all nationalities with sermons in English, Spanish and Italian.

designations.name: Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: The first church on the site, a wooden building of 1891, preached in English, Spanish and Italian. The present church has a three-story tower, a tri-arched entrance, the stone seal of the Redemptorist congregation and stained glass windows; the rectory (1940) and the former St. Joseph's Academy stand on the same block.
heritage.visiting: An active parish; the church is on 11th Avenue at 17th Street.

notes: No parish website read; Mass times not included. The NHL text says the church is at the corner of 11th Avenue and '7th Street' (a typo for 17th).

name: Oxford Exchange
hours_text: Monday–Friday 7:30 AM–5:30 PM; Saturday–Sunday 8 AM–5:30 PM.
summary: A bookstore, gift shop, restaurant and coffee and tea bars in an 1891 building across Kennedy Boulevard from the former Tampa Bay Hotel. It opened in 2012.
quote: Oxford Exchange is not a static space. it evolves and is enriched by every person who enters.

heritage.story: The building dates to 1891 and stands across from the former Tampa Bay Hotel. From the 1920s it held an arcade of local shops and businesses, then stood empty for decades before siblings Blake Casper and Allison Adams reopened it as Oxford Exchange on September 24, 2012.
heritage.visiting: The shop, bookstore, restaurant and coffee and tea bars are open daily.

parking_text: Metered street parking (ParkMobile), a paid attendant lot at First Church of Christ Scientist, and free weekend parking at 606 W Kennedy Blvd (Sat–Sun 9 AM–5:30 PM).
notes: Also a restaurant: the eat-tampa slice may hold the same id. Area: across from the University of Tampa / Plant Museum, filed downtown-tampa like Plant Hall (SPEC 4.1). Verified 2026-09-27: hours, parking, the 1891 building, 1920s arcade, Casper and Adams and the Sept 24, 2012 opening re-read. Coordinates moved to the OSM feature.

hours_text: Lunch Monday–Saturday 11 AM–2:30 PM; Sunday brunch buffet 10:30 AM–2:30 PM; dinner Sunday–Thursday 5:30–9 PM, Friday–Saturday 5:30–10 PM.
summary: A seafood restaurant at the Grand Hyatt Tampa Bay, open since 1986, with floor-to-ceiling windows and a patio on Old Tampa Bay, a Sunday brunch buffet and a private dock for guests arriving by boat.
quote: A Tampa Bay favorite since 1986, Oystercatchers offers fresh seafood, coastal-inspired cuisine, and waterfront dining overlooking the sparkling waters of Tampa Bay.
notes: Added by the verifier (2026-09-27). Inside the grand-hyatt-tampa-bay stay (stays-tampa-outer), whose record names the restaurant. Hours from the Hours & Location page; coordinates are the OpenStreetMap restaurant feature.

name: Palace of Florence Apartments
summary: A 1925 Mediterranean Revival apartment building with a four-story battlemented tower, modeled on Florence's Palazzo Vecchio as part of D. P. Davis's plan for an Italian-style island suburb. It is private apartments.

heritage.architect: M. Leo Elliott, from a concept by artist Athos Menaboni (builder Island Construction Co.)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Mediterranean Revival Style Buildings of Davis Islands MPS)
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Developer D. P. Davis turned Big and Little Grassy Islands into Davis Islands in the 1920s and built in the Mediterranean Revival style throughout. Italian-born artist Athos Menaboni conceived this building, using the Palazzo Vecchio and Palazzo del Podestà as inspiration; its north and south sections are divided by a recessed tile-paved courtyard. The National Register nomination for North Franklin Street notes that financial backing for the Davis Islands venture collapsed in 1926.
heritage.visiting: Private apartments; view it from Davis Boulevard.

notes: Architect: the City book names M. Leo Elliott; NPGallery lists Menaboni, Athos et al. Wikipedia counts 28 units and a 2002–2003 restoration.

name: Palladium at St. Petersburg College
summary: St. Petersburg College's downtown performing arts venue in a 1925 church building, with a concert hall (Hough Hall) and the Side Door Cabaret for jazz, blues, classical, theater, opera and comedy. It is closed for a major renovation and expects to reopen in fall 2027.
quote: The Palladium at SPC is currently undergoing a major renovation and anticipates reopening in fall 2027.

heritage.style: Arts and Crafts details, with tilework by Ernest A. Batchelder
heritage.story: The building was constructed in 1925 as the First Church of Christ, Scientist, designed by Howard Lovewell Cheney. In the late 1990s arts philanthropists turned it into a performing arts center, keeping much of its historic character, and it opened as the Palladium Theater in 1998. It became part of St. Petersburg College in 2007. The current renovation replaces Hough Hall's original 1925 seats while preserving the building's character.
heritage.visiting: Closed for renovation until an expected fall 2027 reopening; Palladium programs continue at other locations.

status_note: Closed for a major renovation; the Palladium says it anticipates reopening in fall 2027 and the box office has no walk-up service (checked Sep 27, 2026).
notes: Contact page: 253 Fifth Avenue North; box office (727) 822-3590; no walk-up service during renovations. The about page mentions its 'historical designation' without naming it; no designation record was found, so none is listed. Verifier 2026-09-27: about, seating and contact pages re-read; every fact and the quote confirmed (fall 2027 reopening; no walk-up box office).

name: Palm Harbor Museum
hours_text: Thursday, Friday and Saturday 10am–2pm; closed on holidays.
price_text: Free or donation; docent-led or self-guided.
summary: Small museum of the history of Palm Harbor, Crystal Beach, Ozona and Curlew from 1800s settlement to today, in a house built around 1915, at the corner of Belcher and Curlew roads.
quote: We welcome you! Free/Donation Tours can be docent-led or self-guided
parking_text: Free parking; enter from Curlew Road.
notes: Hours differ: the museum's site says Thu–Sat 10–2, Visit St. Pete/Clearwater says Wed–Fri 10–2; the museum's own site is used. The ~1915 house date is from the VSPC listing.

name: Palma Ceia Spring (Fred Ball Park)
summary: A small bayside park around a walled natural spring that drew swimmers from about 1903, when Thomas and Ruby Palmer opened Palmera Spring. The spring still flows; a 2025 marker tells how it gave the Palma Ceia neighborhood its name.

heritage.story: Thomas and Ruby Palmer welcomed visitors to their spring-fed pools, a three-mile streetcar ride along Bayshore from downtown, and are credited with naming the area Palma Ceia. A large pool was built in 1928; the county bought the land in the mid-1940s and named it Fred Ball Park, and the City of Tampa acquired it in 1955. Polluted groundwater and backyard pools led to the pool's closing, and volunteers from the Tampa Garden Club's Rose Circle later restored one of the springs with a fountain, walkway and benches.
heritage.visiting: A small public park on Bayshore Boulevard; the spring is inside a concrete wall and the marker is in the park.

name: Palmerin Hotel
summary: A 1925 Mediterranean Revival hotel by architect Martin L. Hampton, one of the most visible survivors of D. P. Davis's original Davis Islands. It is now an elder care facility.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Mediterranean Revival Style Buildings of Davis Islands MPS)
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The City of Tampa counts the Palmerin among 20 remaining Mediterranean Revival buildings on Davis Islands listed on the National Register as examples of Florida's 1920s boom, and calls it one of the most important visible survivors of the subdivision founded by D. P. Davis.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only; it houses an elder care facility.

name: Palmetto Historical Park
hours_text: Tuesday–Friday and the 1st and 3rd Saturdays, 10:00am–12:00pm and 1:00pm–4:00pm. Free guided tour at 11 a.m. (January–April: Tuesdays, Fridays and 1st and 3rd Saturdays). Agricultural Museum: Tuesday–Friday and 1st and 3rd Saturdays, 10 AM–4 PM.
price_text: Free admission and tours
summary: A free Manatee County history park in Palmetto with the 1914 Carnegie Library, Palmetto's first free-standing post office (1880), a circa-1900 cottage museum, a 1920s schoolhouse, a replica chapel and a military museum in a WWII-era Longboat Key house. Next door, the Manatee County Agricultural Museum covers the county's farming history.
quote: Palmetto's Carnegie Library was one of the first libraries built in South Florida.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Palmetto Historic District)

heritage.story: In 1982 a group led by Josephine Harrison organized to save Palmetto's original post office, built about 1880 for postmaster Mary Nettles, and moved it to the corner of 10th Avenue and 6th Street West, the former site of the town's first city hall and school; it was dedicated as Heritage Station in 1983. Andrew Carnegie contributed 10,000 dollars toward the 1914 Carnegie Library, which later served as town hall and school library and now holds the local history archives. A 1984 survey led to the listing of the surrounding Palmetto Historic District in the National Register in 1986.
heritage.visiting: Start upstairs in the Carnegie Library; the other buildings are kept locked and are seen on the free 11 am guided tour. The Manatee County Agricultural Museum is also in the park.

parking_text: Parking lot at 1037 6th St W.
notes: Merged from around-daytrips (verified) + history-region; owner around-daytrips. | [around-daytrips] Added by the verifier (2026-09-27). Run by the Manatee County Clerk's Historical Resources Department. The Agricultural Museum is at 1015 6th Street West, phone (941) 721-2034. The tours page gives May-December tour days as daily when open; the tour-schedule notice gives Tuesday-Friday and 1st/3rd Saturdays. | [history-region] Run under an interlocal agreement involving the Manatee County Clerk's Historical Resources Department. The tours page gives two schedules: 'Tuesdays, Fridays & the 1st and 3rd Saturdays of the month at 11:00 AM due to school programming' (Sept–May) and '11:00 AM every day that the park is open'. The park's story page says the district was listed Dec 30, 1986; NRIS gives Nov 6, 1986; only the year is used. Shared id with around-daytrips (added by its verifier the same day).

name: Paradise Grille (Pass-a-Grille)
hours_text: Daily 7 AM to half an hour after sunset
summary: Casual cafe on the sand at Pass-a-Grille Beach serving breakfast, lunch, dinner, beer and wine, with singer-songwriters playing Friday to Sunday and a crowd for the sunset. A second Paradise Grille is at 6850 Beach Plaza, St. Pete Beach.
quote: Paradise Grille is THE place to catch a famous Florida sunset, meet with friends or enjoy a fantastic meal.

name: Parkesdale Market
hours_text: December to March: open 7 days a week, 9 am to 6 pm. April to November: Wednesday to Sunday, 9 am to 6 pm. Closed on major holidays and for a summer break (July 4 to August 4, 2026).
summary: A family-run farm market off I-4 exit 17, opened in 1969, selling strawberries, citrus, produce, jams and plants, plus strawberry shortcake and strawberry milkshakes. The market says it is busiest November through April, in strawberry season; its site says shortcake returns January 2.
quote: Parkesdale Market is Home to the World Famous Strawberry Shortcake
notes: Merged from around-daytrips + eat-tampa; owner around-daytrips. | [around-daytrips] Only service animals allowed inside, per the market's page. | [eat-tampa] Same id as the around-daytrips record (merge unites them); kind kept as market to match. The plan-your-visit page says Cheryl and Jim Meeks opened the market in February 1969; the homepage banner says 'Family owned since 1968'. The farm itself dates to 1956, when the Parke family planted its first 10 acres of strawberries in Plant City (site).

name: Parkshore Grill
hours_text: Mon–Thu 11 AM–9:30 PM; Fri–Sat 11 AM–10:30 PM; Sun 10:30 AM–9:30 PM
summary: Modern American restaurant on Beach Drive since 1996, with outdoor tables and waterfront views, serving lunch, dinner and weekend brunch under executive chef Tyson Grant. It says it was the first major restaurant on Beach Drive.
quote: Welcome to Parkshore Grill, a Beach Drive icon in downtown St. Petersburg since 1996.

name: Parque Amigos de José Martí
summary: A small walled park on the site of the home of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso, Black Cubans who sheltered José Martí in 1893. It was developed in 1960, has a statue of Martí, and is technically Cuban property, according to the NHL nomination.

heritage.story: The park occupies the site of the house of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso, two Black Cubans who sheltered Martí when Spanish assassins were sent to Ybor City in search of him in 1893. The house burned in the late 1950s and the park was developed in 1960; it has a larger-than-life statue of Martí and a plaque with a medallion portrait of Paulina Pedroso. USF Libraries records that Los Libres Pensadores, forerunner of La Unión Martí-Maceo, held its first official meeting at the Pedroso home on October 26, 1900.
heritage.visiting: An open-air park at 8th Avenue and 13th Street, a block from the Ybor factory; the Martí statue and Pedroso plaque are inside the walls.

notes: Opening hours not found on an official page.

name: Historic Pasco County Courthouse
summary: Pasco County's 1909 courthouse in downtown Dade City, designed by Edward Columbus Hosford. It is on the National Register and the city's historic register.

heritage.architect: Edward Columbus Hosford (built by the Mutual Construction Company)
heritage.style: Classical Revival (NRIS; Wikipedia describes it as Beaux-Arts)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Dade City Historic Register (Old Pasco County Courthouse and Bandstand)

heritage.story: Georgia architect Edward Columbus Hosford designed the courthouse, which the Mutual Construction Company built in 1909 on Meridian Avenue; the National Park Service record gives 1909 and 1920 as its significant years. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on September 20, 2006, and Dade City's municipal historic register includes the old courthouse and its bandstand. In recent years the county clerk has held free Valentine's Day weddings on its steps.
heritage.visiting: In downtown Dade City at 37918 Meridian Avenue; seen from the street.

notes: Separate record for the courthouse; around-daytrips' historic-downtown-dade-city covers the district. Coordinates from Wikipedia (28°21′52″N 82°11′19″W); Photon matched the address to an OSM school node at the same spot, and Census found no match. Verifier (2026-09-27): Nominatim's OSM address point for 37918 Meridian Ave (28.364089, -82.188666) matches the Wikipedia coordinate.

name: Pass-a-Grille Beach
address: Gulf Way, from 1st Avenue to 22nd Avenue
price_text: Metered parking along Gulf Boulevard and Gulf Way.
