name: Pass-a-Grille Historic District
summary: The old beach town at the southern tip of St. Pete Beach, listed in the National Register in 1989 and expanded in 2003. The city publishes a self-guided walking tour of 21 of its historic buildings.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
National Register of Historic Places (Pass-a-Grille Historic District boundary increase)

heritage.story: Zephaniah Phillips, Pass-a-Grille's first homesteader, claimed 79 acres here in 1886; the city's tour says the house at 101 Eighth Avenue incorporates part of his cabin. Residents voted to incorporate at a town meeting on February 2, 1911, and in 1957 Pass-a-Grille was consolidated with Don CeSar, Belle Vista and St. Petersburg Beach into the City of St. Petersburg Beach. The Pass-a-Grille Community Church was dedicated on Christmas Day 1917; its later owner, Joan Haley, left it to Pinellas County in 1989 for a museum of the barrier islands. The district was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on October 19, 1989, with 97 historic buildings, and expanded in 2003.
heritage.visiting: Follow the city's self-guided walking tour (an online story map of 21 buildings). Eighth Avenue keeps early commercial buildings such as the 1912 Merry store at 107 Eighth Avenue.

notes: The tour (City of St. Pete Beach, compiled by Barbara Baker Smith, historian of the Pass-a-Grille Community Church) was read through the ArcGIS item data API (arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/fc43a93a44c64a0e8047b4c2cb9280e8/data). Point is 107 8th Ave, a building on the tour. The former church is the Gulf Beaches Historical Museum per Wikipedia; its own site (gulfbeachesmuseum.org) returned a bot check, so the museum has no record here and its hours/status are unconfirmed. Verifier (2026-09-27): story map re-read through the ArcGIS item-data API: Phillips homestead (79 acres, 1886), the Feb 2, 1911 town meeting, the church dedicated Christmas Day 1917, Joan Haley's 1989 bequest, the 1912 store at 107 Eighth Avenue and the 21-building tour all confirmed; the 1957 consolidation is on the city's Community History page. Added the 2003 boundary increase (ref 03000943) from Wikipedia's infobox.

name: Penny Lane Beatles Museum

quote: The United States' only dedicated Beatles museum, now open in downtown St. Petersburg, Florida.
status_note: Reopened in downtown St. Petersburg in August 2026 after moving from Dunedin (the museum's news page lists 'A Massive Beatles Museum With 1,600 Rare Artifacts Just Opened In St. Pete', Aug 22, 2026). Admission is no longer free, per its visit page.

notes: Hours and ticket prices are dated/dynamic on the site; not recorded.

name: Perry Harvey Sr. Park
hours_text: Sunrise to 10 PM.
summary: A city park that tells the history of the Central Avenue business district, the heart of the Black neighborhood known as The Scrub. Timeline pavers, historic-photo LIFETILES and a Leaders' Row tell the area's history, and the skate park replaces the 1970s Bro Bowl.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Perry Harvey Sr. Park Skateboard Bowl)

heritage.story: The Scrub, Tampa's oldest and largest African American neighborhood, grew up after the Civil War around the Central Avenue Business District. Its single-family homes were demolished in 1959 for the Central Park Village housing project, and I-4 and 1960s urban renewal disrupted Central Avenue; the Encore development later replaced Central Park Village. The park's original skateboard bowl, opened in 1979 and listed on the National Register in 2013 as the first skatepark on a national register, was demolished in a park renovation and replaced by a design based on it.
heritage.visiting: Open sunrise to 10 PM; follow the timeline pavers and LIFETILES history walk, see the gateway sculptures of musicians and dancers, and skate Bro Bowl 2.0.

notes: GPS coordinates published on the City page. Whether the NRHP listing survives the bowl's demolition is not stated; the verifier should check.

heritage.story: The park holds the Safety Harbor Site, identified with Tocobaga, the 16th-century capital of the Tocobaga people, and the type site of the Safety Harbor culture. Its temple mound, about 150 feet across and 20 feet high, is built of alternating layers of shell and sand; the county calls it the largest remaining mound in the Tampa Bay region. Spanish explorers described the town as the Tocobaga capital, and the site was probably abandoned by 1700. The county acquired the property in 1948, and the site was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1964.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: In 1886 Plant bought land on the Hillsborough River from Jess Hayden, whose house stood in an orange grove; when hotel construction began in 1888 much of the grove was kept, and Plant set aside 60 acres for a garden of streams, ponds and some 150 varieties of rare and exotic plants. The university says the original Victorian strolling garden is still intact, and the Friends of Plant Park restored parts of it from 1993 to 2018.

heritage.story: Lakeland businessman John E. Melton planned the building; the Publix Theatre Corporation bought the unfinished theater, and architect J.E. In 1982 citizens formed a nonprofit and bought the theater for $300,000; a major restoration was completed in October 1999.

summary: John and Mable Ringling's bayfront estate in Sarasota, left to the people of Florida and run by Florida State University: an art museum with 21 galleries of European paintings, the Circus Museum, the Historic Asolo Theater, the Bayfront Gardens and Ca' d'Zan, the Ringlings' 1926 Mediterranean Revival mansion.

heritage.architect: Dwight James Baum (Ca' d'Zan); John H. Phillips (Museum of Art)
heritage.style: Mediterranean Revival (Ca' d'Zan); Italianate (Museum of Art)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Caples'-Ringlings' Estates Historic District)

heritage.story: Circus owner John Ringling and his wife Mable commissioned architect Dwight James Baum in 1924 to design Ca' d'Zan, their winter home on Sarasota Bay; the 56-room mansion was completed in late 1926. The museum's charter was established in 1927, its pink Italianate building was finished in 1928, and it opened to the public in 1930. John Ringling left the estate and his art collection to the State of Florida when he died in 1936; Ca' d'Zan opened to the public in 1946, and Florida State University took over the museum in 2000. Hurricanes Helene and Milton damaged Ca' d'Zan in 2024, and restoration is continuing.
heritage.visiting: One ticket covers the Museum of Art, the Circus Museum and the Bayfront Gardens; Ca' d'Zan's first floor is an add-on and its upper floors are seen on a guided tour.

status_note: Ca' d'Zan is open for a self-guided first-floor visit and guided tours while restoration continues after the 2024 hurricanes. The Historic Circus Galleries close November 3–9, 2026 for maintenance.

summary: A free railroad museum in historic downtown Plant City, in the 1909 Union Depot, with railroad artifacts, vintage trains and a caboose, and a train viewing platform where you can watch trains pass.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: The Plant City Union Depot was built in 1908–1909 for the Atlantic Coast Line and Seaboard Air Line railroads; farmers shipped nearly 4 million quarts of strawberries through it in 1926. Passenger service ended in 1971. When the city threatened to demolish it in 1974, the Plant City Arts Council saved it, and it was added to the National Register in 1975. It reopened as a railroad museum in September 2013 and was named in February 2014 for Robert W. Willaford, who donated 28 railroad items to it.

heritage.story: A frame church named St. Louis was built on this site in 1859, and the parish was constituted in 1860. Jesuits took over the parish in 1888 after yellow fever killed three pastors; they broke ground for the present church on February 16, 1898, and dedicated it on January 15, 1905, renaming the parish Sacred Heart. Jesuit High School began in the church's sacristy in 1899. Franciscan friars took over the parish in 2005.

heritage.story: Judge Edmund F. Dunne founded the Catholic Colony of San Antonio in 1882, and Father Gerard Pilz arrived in 1886 as the first Benedictine in Florida. Abbot Francis Sadlier commissioned the Church of the Holy Cross in 1935; designed by Tampa architect Frank Parziole, it was consecrated on January 29, 1948. The abbey's historic district was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1998.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: S. H. Kress opened its first Tampa store in 1904; this building, with nearly identical facades on Franklin Street and Florida Avenue faced in terra cotta that imitates granite, was one of downtown's most popular stores for decades. The block it shares with the former F. W. Woolworth and J. J. Newberry stores is known as the Kress block; students' 1960 lunch-counter sit-ins at the Woolworth store are marked on the corner of Polk and Franklin. Wikipedia reports that the Wilson Company bought the block in 2017 with plans to preserve and redevelop it.

summary: Historic waterfront along Dodecanese Boulevard, center of Tarpon Springs' Greek sponge industry: docked sponge boats, sponge and souvenir shops, Greek restaurants and bakeries, sponge-diving exhibits, and sightseeing and dolphin cruises on the Anclote River.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Tarpon Springs Sponge Exchange)

heritage.story: After Tarpon Springs was incorporated in 1887, John Cheney, a promoter associated with Hamilton Disston, began harvesting sponges from the Gulf, and by 1890 the industry was established. Experienced divers from Greece followed, using rubberized suits and helmets; by 1905 more than 500 Greek sponge divers worked from 50 boats. Sponge buyers built the Sponge Exchange in 1907, a courtyard building where catches were stored for twice-weekly auctions. The Greektown Historic District, about 140 acres around the docks, was listed in 2014 as the first Traditional Cultural Property in Florida.
heritage.visiting: Walk Dodecanese Boulevard past docked sponge boats, sponge shops, Greek restaurants and bakeries; the Sponge Exchange now holds more than 30 shops and restaurants, and SpongeDocks.net says sponge auctions are held weekly.

notes: Merged from see-pinellas + history-region; owner see-pinellas. | [see-pinellas] spongedocks.net is a local commercial guide, not a public body; phone and hours from the VSPC listing. 'on the Anclote River' from the spongedocks.net cruise text ('through the Anclote River and out to the Gulf'). The Sponge Exchange's NRHP ref 72000348 (listed 1972) comes from Wikipedia's Pinellas NRHP list; its NPGallery page returned no metadata. Four sponge boats (Duchess, George N. Cretekos, N. K. Symi, St. Nicholas III and VI) are also separately listed (1990) per the same list. SpongeDocks.net says 'For 30 years, the sponge industry was the largest industry in Florida'; not repeated as fact. designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The House of Prayer congregation was organized in 1908 and grew under William Conckling Richardson, which led to this sanctuary; through the 1920s and 1940s it was the third largest Episcopal church in Tampa. The City of Tampa says it is one of two identified buildings in Florida built with chert as a structural material. Wikipedia reports that in 1997 the congregation merged with St. James Episcopal Church, founded in 1892 to serve Tampa's Black population, whose site was taken for the new Blake High School.

summary: The domed 1943 cathedral of Tarpon Springs' Greek Orthodox parish, paid for in part by sponge divers' harvests. It leads the city's Epiphany celebration each January 6.

heritage.story: Greek immigrants built the parish's first church, a frame building, in 1907 and named it for Saint Nicholas, protector of seafaring people. The current cathedral was completed in 1943; its marble from Mount Penteli, a gift of the Greek government, had first been shipped to New York for the 1939 World's Fair. The church was elevated to a cathedral in January 1979. Each January 6 the parish holds its Epiphany celebration, when young men dive into Spring Bayou to retrieve a cross.
heritage.visiting: Visitors are welcome; the cathedral is typically open for prayer on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Public parking lots are a block away.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Josiah Richardson built the 214-foot tower over a spring on the Hillsborough River, with a 150,000-gallon tank; it was the area's main water source until the early 1970s. By the 1920s Sulphur Springs was a popular destination reached by streetcar from Tampa, with medicinal waters, an alligator farm, a pool, a toboggan slide and a dance hall. Richardson also built the octagonal 1925 gazebo over the spring itself (701 E. Bird Street), a separate City landmark.
heritage.visiting: See it from North Florida Avenue near the Hillsborough River.

summary: A city-owned botanical garden in a drained sinkhole, begun by plumber George Turner Sr. and run by his family for almost 100 years; paths wind past tropical plants, waterfalls, flamingos and rehomed tropical birds, and a History Center tells its roadside-attraction story.

designations.name: St. Petersburg Local Historic Landmark
National Register of Historic Places (historic main entrance)

heritage.story: George Turner Sr., a plumber and gardener, bought the land in 1911, drained the sinkhole called Curlew Pond with clay tiles and by the early 1930s charged fifteen cents for tours. His sons brought the first flamingos in 1955, and the family ran the gardens as a roadside attraction for three generations before putting them up for sale in 1989. St. Petersburg voters approved a one-time tax increase to save them; the gardens became a local historic landmark in 1998, and the main entrance was listed in the National Register in 1999.
heritage.visiting: Open daily except Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day; the History Center is in the original 1940 entrance and gift shop.

The present cable-stayed bridge, designed by Figg & Muller Engineering Group and built by the American Bridge Company, opened in 1987, and the old bridge was partly demolished and turned into two fishing piers.

heritage.story: Designed by John Eberson, the theatre opened on October 15, 1926, inside a ten-story office building on Franklin Street; its auditorium imitates the garden of a Spanish villa under a ceiling of stars, and its Wurlitzer organ is still played. Attendance declined in the 1960s and 1970s and in 1973 the building faced demolition; the City of Tampa rescued it by taking over its leases, the Arts Council of Hillsborough County ran its programming from 1976 to 2010, and it reopened in early 1978. A 2017 renovation reseated the auditorium, reducing capacity from 1,446 to 1,238 seats.

heritage.story: Designed by J. F. Leitner of Wilmington, North Carolina, the station opened on May 15, 1912, to combine the passenger operations of the Atlantic Coast Line, the Seaboard Air Line and the Tampa Northern Railroad; the City notes it was built by a group of businessmen led by Peter O. Knight rather than a railroad company. Its waiting room was segregated when it opened. Ridership fell after the 1950s and the station closed in 1984; a volunteer-led nonprofit raised over $4 million, restoration was completed in May 1998, and CSX donated the station to the City of Tampa that year.
heritage.visiting: The waiting room is open when Amtrak agents are on duty (9:45 AM–6 PM daily). Limited free parking at the station; the City's Twiggs Street Garage is nearby.

heritage.story: A. W. Ormond and his daughter Mary built a cabin near Spring Bayou in 1876, and Mary Ormond named the settlement Tarpon Springs in 1879. Hamilton Disston's 1880 purchase of four million acres of Florida's west coast included the town, which Disston's investment turned into a winter resort for wealthy Northerners; it was incorporated in 1887 with 52 residents. The district around Spring Bayou, bounded by Read, Hibiscus, Orange and Lemon Streets and Levis Avenue, has 145 historic buildings and was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on December 6, 1990.
heritage.visiting: Walk the winding streets around Spring Bayou; the Safford House Museum is in the district.

heritage.story: Chicago businesswoman Bertha Palmer bought the land early in the 1900s as a hunting preserve; after her death in 1918 investors formed two companies to build a golf course and homes and a 5,000-acre orange grove, which the city says was the largest in the world in the 1920s. Tom Bendelow's course opened in 1922 with a clubhouse by M. Leo Elliott, three years before the city was incorporated; the clubhouse became part of Florida College in the 1930s, and the course hosted the first Florida Open in 1925. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2012. The city calls Temple Terrace one of the first golfing communities in the United States and adopted a local historic preservation program in 2023.
heritage.visiting: The course and club are on Inverness Avenue in Temple Terrace; Riverhills Drive along the Hillsborough River dates from 1921.

heritage.story: Fourteen Universalists formed a congregation in Tarpon Springs in 1885 on land donated by Anson P. K. Safford. After fire destroyed its first building, the present church was built in 1908 at Grand Boulevard and Read Street. When a tropical storm broke sanctuary windows on September 28, 1918, George Inness Jr. and his family donated paintings to fill the openings, the start of the church's Inness collection. Sinkhole damage closed the buildings late in 2013; after nearly six years of work the church was rededicated on September 29, 2019.
heritage.visiting: Call or email the church to schedule a tour of the paintings; Sunday services are at 10:30 a.m.

summary: A 3,000-acre county preserve on Tampa Bay in north St. Petersburg where Indigenous people lived for thousands of years. designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Weeden Island Site)

heritage.story: Indigenous peoples lived at the site for thousands of years; the preserve says their descendants developed the Weeden Island culture (an alternate spelling), which lasted some 800 years and is known for ceremonial pottery and burials with grave goods. The Weeden Island Site was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1972. In 2011 archaeologists and volunteers excavated a pine dugout canoe 39.9 feet long from the shoreline; radiocarbon dating placed it between AD 690 and 1010, and it is attributed to the Manasota culture. Later island history includes homesteaders, speakeasies, a Hollywood movie studio and a 1930s airport.
heritage.visiting: The Cultural and Natural History Center has exhibits, programs and tours; the preserve says the public can view the 1,100-year-old canoe in the Welcome Center. More than 4.7 miles of boardwalks and trails cross the preserve.

status_note: Open. Part of the Bay Boardwalk is closed for repairs until late 2026, the north paddling trail is closed, and the preserve is closed until noon on Oct. 24, 2026 for a trail run (county park and park-updates pages).

heritage.story: Hugh C. Macfarlane set out to turn 120 acres of swampland west of the Hillsborough River into a cigar town; his investment company financed the Fortune Street Bridge and built factories and worker housing, and by 1893 West Tampa had 25 cigar factories. It incorporated as a city in 1895, with a population largely of Spanish, Italian and Cuban immigrants, and stayed independent until Tampa annexed it in 1925. Hillsborough County notes that it then had the second largest Hispanic population in Florida.

heritage.story: On February 29, 1960, about 40 students from George S. Middleton and Howard W. After about a week of demonstrations Mayor Julian B. Lane agreed to appoint a biracial committee, and by September 1960 Tampa's lunch counters were integrated. Hillsborough County says the store closed in the early 1990s and the building is vacant; the marker was erected in 2018.

Former mayor Abram C. Pheil won the first round-trip ticket at auction with a bid of 400 dollars, and the service ran from January to May 1914. The city's markers list records two bronze plaques on a stone monument at the start of the pier approach on 2nd Avenue NE: one erected January 1, 1938, and one dedicated December 4, 1953, reading 'From this site, the St. Petersburg - Tampa Airboat Line, the world's first scheduled airline, began regular flights between St. Petersburg and Tampa, Jan. 1, 1914.' The St. Pete Pier now lists the spot as Benoist Centennial Plaza featuring the World's First Airline Monument.

name: Ybor City Historic District
aliases: Ybor City National Historic Landmark District
summary: A National Historic Landmark district northeast of downtown Tampa, founded in 1886 as a planned cigar-making town. It keeps cigar factories, immigrant social-club buildings, worker houses and the 7th Avenue commercial strip.
quote: At the turn of the 20th century, nowhere in the United States was as famous for its cigars as Tampa’s Ybor City, which was once known as the “Cigar Capital of the World.”

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
National Historic Landmark District
City of Tampa local historic district

heritage.story: In late 1885 Vicente Martínez-Ybor and Ignacio Haya bought land northeast of Tampa for cigar factories and worker housing; by the end of 1886 both factories were running and several hundred worker houses were occupied, and Tampa annexed Ybor City in June 1887. Cuban, Spanish and Italian immigrants built mutual-aid clubs with cooperative medical plans, and José Martí came here to raise money and support for Cuban independence. The hand-rolled cigar industry declined after the 1920s, and a 1965 urban renewal project leveled 70 acres, including 660 frame houses, before preservation efforts turned the district around. The City of Tampa gives its period of significance as 1886 to 1940.
heritage.visiting: Walk the 7th Avenue commercial strip, which the National Park Service says runs 11 blocks from Nick Nuccio Parkway to 26th Street. The Ybor City Visitor Information Center is in the Centro Ybor complex (1600 E 8th Ave, Suite B104; Monday to Saturday 10 AM–4 PM, Sunday noon–4 PM), and the Ybor City Museum State Park is on 9th Avenue.

notes: Coordinates are the district point from Wikipedia's NRHP list. Built = the City's period of significance (1886–1940); the NPS says most buildings date from 1886 to World War I. NHL district year 1990 from the City designations book.

quote: The museum, housed in the historic Ferlita Bakery, traces the rich cultural history of Ybor City and the cigar-making industry.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Francisco Ferlita, a Sicilian-born baker, founded La Joven Francesca bakery in Ybor City in 1896, and it baked Cuban bread for the neighborhood. After a fire in 1922 the bakery was rebuilt with a second brick oven, and it made bread until 1973. The building was acquired in 1976 and opened as a museum in September 1980; the brick ovens are still inside. The Ybor City Chamber says the Ferlita Bakery building is listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
heritage.visiting: Self-guided exhibits with written and audio information and a video; guided tours of La Casita on request; the ornamental garden.

parking_text: Street parking is limited; the TECO Line Streetcar stops in Ybor City.

name: V. M. Ybor Cigar Factory (Ybor Factory Building)
summary: The red brick cigar factory Vicente Martínez-Ybor completed in 1886, the first factory of the planned town of Ybor City. José Martí spoke from its 14th Street steps in 1893; the building is now privately owned offices.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: Ybor's factory at 14th Street and 9th Avenue was completed in 1886; a second factory (the Stemmery) and a warehouse followed in 1902, filling most of the block between 8th and 9th Avenues and 13th and 14th Streets. In 1893 José Martí spoke from the factory's cast-iron steps, urging cigar workers to join the fight for Cuban independence; the original portico was taken to Havana and the present one is a reproduction. After Ybor died in 1896 the plant passed to the Havana America Company (1899), the American Cigar Company (1901) and Hav-A-Tampa (1954), and in the 1970s it became the Ybor Square shopping mall.
heritage.visiting: Private property: view the exterior and the reproduction portico on 14th Street (Avenida República de Cuba). Wikipedia reports that the building became offices in 2002 and that the Church of Scientology bought it in 2010.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: David Levy Yulee, who in 1845 became the first American of Jewish heritage to serve in the U.S. Senate, ran a 5,000-acre plantation on the Homosassa River worked by about 1,000 enslaved African Americans. Its steam-powered mill ran from 1851 to 1864, making sugar, syrup and molasses, and supplied sugar to Confederate soldiers during the Civil War. In May 1864 Union forces burned Yulee's plantation and home but did not find the mill, which was then abandoned and fell into ruin. The site was listed on the National Register in 1970.
heritage.visiting: An outdoor ruins site with the mill's stone foundation, well, 40-foot chimney, iron gears and cane press. Hours and fees are on the Florida State Parks site, which could not be read on Sep 27, 2026.
